query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In equiatomic CrFeCoNiAl alloys, the presence of Al promotes the in situ formation of a thin, coherent Al2O3 scale at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidizing/corrosive atmospheres, thereby suppressing the spallation seen in CrFeCoNiMn alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrFeCoNiAl high-entropy alloy produced as a single-phase solid solution via arc melting and homogenized heat treatment.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to isothermal oxidation at 900 °C in a controlled atmosphere (e.g., 20% O2/80% inert gas) for 24 hours.
generation.conditions: Test temperature >900 °C under a well-controlled oxygen partial pressure in an oxidative and/or corrosive environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, sub-micron (≈1 μm) Al2O3 layer at the metal/oxide interface.
generation.mechanism: Lower effective diffusivity and higher thermodynamic stability of Al2O3 compared to Mn-oxides reduce additional cation transport and suppress spallation, resulting in a coherent protective layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline CrFeCoNiMn alloy, the Al-alloy will exhibit a thinner, adherent oxide scale with lower incidence of cracking/spallation and lower overall oxidation rate (parabolic rate constant reduced by an order of magnitude).
generation.baseline: Equiatomic CrFeCoNiMn alloy processed under identical conditions, known to form unstable, porous, and spalling Mn-rich oxide scales.
generation.boundary: Applicable for single-phase solid-solution states in high-entropy alloys exposed at temperatures above 900 °C; the effect may be limited if significant microsegregation occurs.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative threshold of Al content required and potential competitive oxidation with Cr may introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare both CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiMn alloys under identical processing conditions and subject them to 900 °C oxidation in a controlled 20% O2 atmosphere for 24 hours.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/TEM imaging to measure oxide scale thickness and continuity
XRD and EDS analyses to identify oxide phases
Adhesion/spallation tests to assess scale integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrFeCoNiAl alloy does not exhibit a significantly thinner, more coherent oxide scale and reduced spallation compared to the CrFeCoNiMn alloy, the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The oxidation behaviour of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA provides valuable insights into its suitability for high-temperature applications. This oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi HEA plays a critical role in determining its mechanical, thermal, and corrosion resistance properties in elevated temperature environments. The observed non-protective oxide formation, particularly the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy, can have significant implications for this particular alloy’s mechanical properties. Mn is known to contribute to solid solution strengthening and can enhance the mechanical strength and ductility of alloys. Therefore, the formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures.

At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides. papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMn-based and CoCrFeNiMn/Al-doped HEAs (relevant to CrFeCoNiX with X = Mn or Al)
papers.approach: Combined experimental techniques including in situ atom probe tomography, high‐resolution electron microscopy, X‐ray diffraction, and XANES; analysis guided by a preferential interactivity parameter (PIP).
papers.findings: At high temperatures (>900 °C), the oxidation process develops a layered oxide structure with an inner zone enriched in slower-diffusing elements (e.g. Cr) and an outer zone dominated by fast diffusing species (e.g. Mn). The presence of Al leads to the formation of slower-growing, more stable Al2O3 scales. The work highlights that atomic properties (atomic size, redox potential) largely dictate which oxides form and when composition inversion (TOCI) occurs during prolonged oxidation.
papers.mechanism: Differential elemental diffusivity and oxidation potential govern which species reach the oxide/metal interface. Fast-diffusing Mn tends to form non-protective, volatile or porous oxides, whereas the slower kinetics of Cr and Al (especially when present in sufficient amounts) favor formation of protective, coherent scales (Cr2O3 or Al2O3).

papers.title: Thermodynamic Insights into the Oxidation Mechanisms of CrMnFeCoNi High-Entropy Alloy Using In Situ X-ray Diffraction.
papers.system: CrMnFeCoNi HEA (the so-called Cantor alloy, representative for systems where X = Mn)
papers.approach: In situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction experiments coupled with thermodynamic (CALPHAD) calculations.
papers.findings: The study found that Mn is the dominant oxide-forming element, leading to the early formation of Mn2O3 that is porous and non-protective, eventually resulting in depletion of Mn from the bulk alloy. Protective Cr2O3 was not observed under the tested conditions, and the dynamic evolution of phases suggested that elemental diffusion sequences (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni) play a critical role.
papers.mechanism: Fast outward diffusion of Mn compared to other elements leads to the formation of unstable, cracking oxide layers. The mechanism emphasizes that a competition between oxygen inward diffusion and cation outward diffusion, dictated by individual element mobilities and thermodynamic driving forces, governs the stability of the oxide scale.

papers.title: Influence of the Al Content on the Properties of Mechanically Alloyed CoCrFeNiMnXAl20-X High-Entropy Alloys.
papers.system: CoCrFeNiMnXAl alloys (directly addressing systems where X = Mn versus higher Al content)
papers.approach: Mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering, with systematic variation of Al content; subsequent oxidation testing and microstructural characterization.
papers.findings: Alloys with lower Al content (e.g. Mn15Al5) developed thick, porous, and internally oxidized layers with sub-surface porosity due to Mn diffusion, whereas alloys with higher Al content formed a very thin (~1 µm), coherent, and protective Al-rich oxide scale without interfacial spallation.
papers.mechanism: Increasing Al content shifts the oxidation mechanism from one driven by rapid Mn diffusion (leading to unstable manganese oxides) to one in which the formation of an AlxOy protective layer occurs. This scale effectively blocks further oxidation by suppressing metal cation diffusion.

papers.title: Modeling Oxidation of AlCoCrFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Using Stochastic Cellular Automata.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA (relevant for X = Al in CrFeCoNiX alloys)
papers.approach: Simulation using a stochastic cellular automata model that incorporates diffusion coefficients (from molecular simulations) and microstructural features (single-crystal vs. dendritic/interdendritic structures).
papers.findings: The modeling predicts parabolic oxidation kinetics with formation of protective α-Al2O3 and Cr2O3 scales in single-crystal configurations, while phase-separated (dendritic) microstructures lead to spatial segregation of oxides. The simulation results correlate with experimental observations regarding the influence of microstructure on the uniformity and stability of the oxide layer.
papers.mechanism: The competition between bulk diffusion and localized phase segregation determines the structure of the oxide scale. In homogeneous microstructures, the uniform distribution of elements favors the development of protective scales; in contrast, heterogeneous structures cause regions of differing oxidation behavior.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: AlCoCrFeNi HEA with refined (ultrafine) grain microstructure (again relevant for X = Al systems)
papers.approach: Experimental evaluation of oxidation kinetics, grain structure (via processing-induced grain refinement), and cross-sectional oxide layer analysis under high temperature (900–1050 °C) oxidation conditions.
papers.findings: The introduction of ultrafine grains (high grain-boundary density) improves oxidation resistance by promoting rapid formation of a dense, adherent Cr-rich and subsequently Al2O3 inner oxide layers. The parabolic rate constants and activation energy measurements indicate a slowed oxidation process compared to coarser-grained (as-cast) samples.
papers.mechanism: Grain refinement enhances intergranular diffusion pathways that favor the rapid development of a continuous, protective oxide layer. The diffusion of chromium cations through the dense network of grain boundaries is pivotal in forming a stable barrier against further oxidation.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA (providing insights into systems where X = Mn; note absence of Ni can serve as a baseline comparison)
papers.approach: 3D laser printing to produce the alloy followed by isothermal oxidation tests at 700 °C and 900 °C, with phase and microstructural analysis via XRD and microscopic characterization.
papers.findings: At 900 °C, the alloy exhibited spallation of the oxide scale accompanied by the formation of Mn-rich spinels and mixed oxides (e.g., MnFe2O4, MnFeO2, and Cr2O3). Cracks and voids were observed, indicating unstable oxidation behavior at higher temperatures, in contrast to better stability at lower temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Rapid diffusion of Mn promotes the formation of non-protective, volatile oxide phases and undermines the development of coherent, protective oxide layers. The imbalance in cation diffusion (with Mn diffusing much faster than Co and others) is central to the observed spallation and cracking.

established: Elemental diffusivities and oxidation potentials govern which oxide phases form; fast-diffusing elements like Mn tend to form less protective, spalling oxides.
Protective oxide layers, such as Cr2O3 and especially Al2O3, are key for oxidation resistance at high temperatures.
The microstructure (grain size, phase distribution) significantly influences diffusion pathways and therefore the oxidation kinetics and scale stability.

approaches_tried.approach: In situ characterization using HTXRD, APT, and XANES to capture real-time phase evolutions during oxidation.
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified phase transformations and spatial distributions in oxide scales; established roles of individual elements.

approaches_tried.approach: Computational modeling via stochastic cellular automata to simulate mesoscale oxide growth in single-crystal and dendritic microstructures.
approaches_tried.outcome: Predicted oxide compositions and scale morphologies that closely match experimental observations, highlighting the importance of microstructure.

approaches_tried.approach: Microstructural tailoring (e.g., grain refinement via high strain rate processing) as a means to enhance protective oxide formation.
approaches_tried.outcome: Ultrafine-grained samples exhibited higher oxidation resistance due to formation of dense, protective oxide layers.

mechanisms: Differential cation diffusion rates (Mn > Cr > Fe > Co > Ni) dictate which elements reach the surface to form oxides.
Thermodynamic preferences (e.g., lower free energies for Al2O3 formation) yield more stable and coherent protective scales when the element is sufficiently present.
Microstructural features such as grain boundaries enhance or hinder the effective diffusion of metal cations, affecting oxide scale coherence.
disagreements: Some studies (e.g., the in situ HTXRD work on CrMnFeCoNi) did not observe the formation of protective Cr2O3 under certain oxidation conditions, while others emphasize its protective role.
There is variability in the oxide sequence and protective qualities between single-phase and multiphase (or segregated) structures, with debates on which elemental contributions are dominant.
open_questions: How does the addition of Si (the X = Si case) modify the oxidation mechanism in CrFeCoNiX alloys, particularly in terms of oxide phase stability and diffusion kinetics?
What are the precise differences in oxidation behavior between single-phase and multiphase solid-solution states in these high-entropy systems above 900 °C?

How do controlled microstructural variables (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) interact with compositional effects (Mn vs. Al vs. Si) to govern the formation and persistence of a coherent protective oxide layer?
opportunities: A controlled comparative study of CrFeCoNiX alloys varying X (Si, Mn, and Al) under identical high-temperature oxidative/corrosive exposures to delineate the role of the X element.

Combining in situ high-resolution techniques (HTXRD, APT) with advanced modeling to develop a unified mechanistic hypothesis that quantifies the interplay between elemental diffusivities, oxidation potentials, and microstructure.
Exploring microstructural engineering (e.g., grain refinement) in multiphase versus single-phase HEAs as a pathway to tailor oxide scale stability and test the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.

Investigating falsifying conditions – for instance, if under high-temperature exposure the expected relationship between diffusion rates and oxide scale integrity does not hold, then the hypothesized mechanism would need revision.

directions.direction: Alloying composition design to alter oxide‐forming element kinetics
directions.assessment: By substituting X from Mn to Al or Si, this approach directly targets the key mechanism of differential cation diffusivities and thermodynamic oxide stabilities. Numerous studies support the protective role of Al2O3 and the potential of Si to form stable silicates, while evidence also shows that high Mn promotes spalling. The approach is well grounded in established oxidation kinetics and is feasible with current processing and characterization methods.

directions.direction: Microstructural control via processing (single‐phase vs multiphase)
directions.assessment: Controlling the microstructure to obtain a homogeneous single-phase state versus multiphase segregation addresses the limitation by modifying diffusion pathways and local stress fields that govern oxide coherence versus spallation. Previous evidence on grain boundary and phase segregation effects supports this direction, making it feasible and informative.

directions.direction: Kinetic analysis of cation versus oxygen diffusion
directions.assessment: Focusing on the relative rates of metal cation diffusion (especially of the alloying element X) versus oxygen ingress directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that a balance between these diffusion rates controls oxide scale stability. Simulation and tracer studies are well established in the literature, making this approach informative and directly targeted.

directions.direction: Surface modification to induce pre-oxide layering
directions.assessment: Pre-forming an engineered surface layer can simulate the effect of stable oxide formation and allow controlled comparison against a baseline untreated alloy. While this does not directly modify the bulk diffusion kinetics, it can decouple surface scale formation from intrinsic alloy diffusivities. However, it is slightly less direct in addressing the inherent mechanistic question than the other studies.
